Blood pressure targets should be individualized. For patients with frailty, the systolic blood pressure target should be < 150 mmHg, but not lower than 130 mmHg.

Patients with simple snoring, mild to moderate OSAS, or severe OSAS intolerant to MAD or CPAP; used in combination with other therapies.
PAP therapy: includes CPAP, autoCPAP, BiPAP, autoBiPAP, Adaptive Servo-Ventilation (ASV)

Moderate to severe OSAS; mild OSAS with significant symptoms, or comorbid cardiovascular disease, diabetes; perioperative treatment for OSAS; persistent OSAS after surgery or other treatments; overlap syndrome with coexisting OSAS and COPD.
Patients with simple snoring and mild to moderate OSAS; severe OSAS intolerant to CPAP; used in combination with surgery or non-invasive positive airway pressure therapy for severe OSAS.
Patients with moderate to severe OSAS or those for whom PAP is ineffective or intolerable.
Non-severely obese patients with moderate or mild OSAS; severe OSAS with grade II or above tonsil hypertrophy

autoBiPAP: automatic bilevel positive airway pressure; autoCPAP: automatic continuous positive airway pressure; BiPAP: bilevel positive airway pressure; COPD: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; CPAP: continuous positive airway pressure; MAD: mandibular advancement device; OSAS: obstructive sleep apnea syndrome; PAP: positive airway pressure.
Indomethacin, Ibuprofen, Phenylbutazone, Celecoxib, Oxaprozin, Diclofenac Sodium
(1) Sodium and water retention; (2) reduced circulating prostaglandins; (3) kidney damage.

Blood pressure typically normalizes
after drug discontinuation; if necessary, use antihypertensive drugs such
as CCBs, ACEIs/ARBs.

(1) Block H1 and H2 histamine receptors, reducing histamine-mediated vasodilation; (2) blocking H1 receptor activation also inhibits endothelial cell-derived vasodilators (nitric oxide and prostaglandins).

Blood pressure usually returns to normal after discontinuation of antihistamines; consider using diuretics,
CCBs, ACEIs/ARBs.

Closely monitor for increased heart
rate, arrhythmias, and changes in blood pressure.
Sertraline, Fluvoxamine, Paroxetine, Venlafaxine, Reboxetine, Tranylcypromine, Phenelzine
(1) Depletion of 5-HT and increased free 5-HT levels in the blood; (2) increased sensitivity of myocardium and blood vessels to sympathetic nerve stimulation, leading to hypertension.

Consider switching to other types of
antidepressants or adding beta-blockers, CCBs, or ACEIs.
(1) Increased blood volume; (2) effects on RAS and sympathetic nervous system; (3) effects on renal blood flow; (4) abnormal glucose and lipid metabolism.

Immediately discontinue oral contraceptives; blood pressure typically
returns to normal within 3 to 6 months after discontinuation.

VEGF Monoclonal Antibodies (Bevacizumab), Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (Sunitinib, Sorafenib, Axitinib)

(1) Local activation of RAS; (2) vasoconstriction; (3) increased sensitivity of smooth muscle cells to
endogenous vasopressin; (4) increased blood viscosity.
Use beta-blockers, dihydropyridine CCBs, ARBs; avoid non-dihydropyridine CCBs.
(1) Enhanced RAS hypertensive effects; (2) increased peripheral vascular sensitivity to catecholamines; (3) sodium and water retention.

Consider using potassium-sparing
diuretics, CCBs, beta-blockers, or
ACEIs for hypertension control; closely monitor potassium levels.
(1) Increased endothelin-1 release and thromboxane B2 synthesis; (2) decreased nitric oxide synthesis in vascular endothelium; (3) abnormal peripheral vascular constriction.
CCBs or alpha-blockers are the first choice; diuretics and ACEIs are less effective.
(1) Increased endothelin levels in renal vasculature, decreased glomerular filtration rate; (2) inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis and release.

Licorice extracts, such as Glycyrrhizin, Compound Licorice Tablets, C
holic Acid, Alisecium

(1) Inhibition of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity, leading to cortisol-mediated mineralocorticoid excess and hypertension; (2) inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis; (3) inhibition of histamine synthesis and release.
Blood pressure typically normalizes after drug discontinuation; monitor potassium levels.
Ephedrine Nasal Drops, Ephedrine combined with Chlorpheniramine, Diphenhydramine, etc.
(1) Direct stimulation of adrenal alpha and beta2 receptors; (2) indirect promotion of NE neurotransmitter release; (3) significant central nervous system stimulation.

ACEI: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor; ARB: angiotensin receptor blocker; CCB: calcium channel blocker; 5-HT: 5-hydroxytryptamine (Serotonin); NE: norepinephrine; RAS: renin-angiotensin system; VEGF: vascular endothelial growth factor.

CACNA1H: calcium voltage-gated channel subunit α1H; CUL3: cullin 3 protein; CYP17A1: cytochrome P450 family 17 subfamily A member 1; CYP11B1: cytochrome P450 family 11 subfamily B member 1; CYP11B2: cytochrome P450 family 11 subfamily B member 2; CLCN2: chloride voltage-gated channel 2; EPAS1: endothelial PAS domain-containing protein 1; FH: fumarate hydratase; HSD11B2: 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2; KCNJ5: potassium inwardly rectifying channel subfamily J member 5; KLHL3: Kelch-like protein family member 3; MAX: MYC-associated factor X; NF1: neurofibromin 1; NR3C1: nuclear receptor subfamily 3 group C member 1; PAC: plasma aldosterone concentration; PRA: plasma renin activity; RET: Ret proto-oncogene; SCNN1B: Epithelial sodium channel β subunit; SCNN1G: Epithelial sodium channel γ subunit; SDHA: Succinate dehydrogenase complex subunit A; SDHAF2: Succinate dehydrogenase complex assembly factor 2; SDHB: Succinate dehydrogenase complex subunit B; SDHC: Succinate dehydrogenase complex subunit C; SDHD: Succinate dehydrogenase complex subunit D; TMEM127: Transmembrane protein 127; WNK1: WNK lysine-deficient protein kinase 1; WNK4: WNK lysine-deficient protein kinase 4; VHL: Von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor; ↑ indicates increase, ↓ indicates decrease, - indicates normal levels.

History of hypertension and treatment, use of sympathomimetic drugs and other medications; symptoms such as headache, visual disturbances, neurological symptoms, nausea/vomiting, chest/back pain, cardiovascular/respiratory
symptoms, oliguria, weight changes, etc.

Blood pressure: repeat measurements, consider measuring blood pressure in all four limbs, and postural blood pressure if necessary; pulse, respiration, temperature; assess fluid volume, dehydration, edema; central nervous system: consciousness changes, agitation, hemiplegia; fundoscopy: linear or flame-shaped hemorrhages, exudates, retinal edema, papilledema; neck: jugular venous distension, bruits; chest: cardiac enlargement, tachycardia, murmurs, signs of heart failure; abdomen: liver enlargement, pulsations, masses; extremities: edema, arterial pulses.

Urinalysis, complete blood count (including smear); Blood chemistry (BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, glucose, cardiac
markers, creatine phosphokinase, etc.); ECG, chest X-ray, arterial blood gases (if necessary); Cardiac, abdominal ultrasound, cranial CT or MRI, thoracoabdominal CT if necessary; Plasma renin activity, aldosterone, catecholamines, BNP levels if needed.

(1) Establish personal and family health records, sign up with a family doctor,
and incorporate the patient into standardized hypertension management.

(2) Assess the extent of target organ damage.

and signs.
(3) Determine whether the hypertension is secondary.
(3) Monitor for adverse drug reactions and medication adherence.
(4) Cardiovascular comprehensive risk assessment and determination of intervention methods.
(4) Monitor for related complications and improvements.
(5) Identify barriers to lifestyle changes and medication adherence.
(6) Provide lifestyle guidance and medication therapy.
(7) Assess whether new conditions (e.g., diabetes, renal insufficiency) require medication adjustments.
(8) Monitor and record home blood pressure.
